# 17-expanse — sources

Back-test entry `17-expanse.yaml`: Expanse, job sizes predicted at submit time on shared GPU clusters (YC Spring 2026,
P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC
post of 2026-05-04 and the Launch HN of 2026-06-01 (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era
where one exists; anything later is marked as later and sits under *Status today*).

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Researchers and ML engineers who submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes GPU cluster.
   [LYC] "Running compute on a cluster means guessing memory, time, and GPUs before you submit."
   [HN] "We also flag failures we think are about to happen and surface line-level optimisations the researcher can apply
   themselves." → `roles[researcher]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster.
   [LYC] "Get it wrong and your job fails mid-run. Over-guess and you pay for compute you never use."
   [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work. So everyone over-requests by two to three
   times." → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At every job submission. [HN] "We scan any workloads about to be submitted through SLURM/K8s
   (plugging into the life cycles of the job so you don't have to change how you submit things)". → `context.circumstance`,
   `occasion: job submission`. Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (several submissions a working day) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; Prevalence `p_80_100` ("everyone over-requests").

4. **Which people.** Researchers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs, at national HPC centres, AI labs,
   quant funds and drug discovery.
   [HN] "If you run a HPC/GPU cluster (SLURM or K8s, 100+ GPUs), we'd love to have a talk." [LYC] "Know anyone in AI
   infrastructure (managing cloud and/or on-premise data centres), quant finance, drug discovery, or AI research labs?"
   → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (rule U); the founders are in Edinburgh and the cluster they
   measured is a national-scale HPC site, and their ask names no country.

5. **Who pays.** The cluster's operator, per cluster; a department runs the paid pilot.
   [HN] "We offer a two-week measurement window where we install, ingest, and report recoverable capacity to datacenter
   operators, followed by a paid pilot deployment in one department at a fixed monthly fee, renewing at the same rate
   unless the scope expands." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: operator}`; Buyer and payer tests "The department head"
   (the author's reading of "in one department"), "The security team" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A security
   review of an agent on every node", from [HN] "Expanse installs on every node" and the thread's security objection
   ("Any competent enterprise risk team is going to give a hard no to a SaaS application being in the critical path for
   on-prem business critical workloads.") with the founder's reply ("Deployments are air-gapped and run in the customer's
   VPC, on their own hardware."); "Letting it read job scripts and source code" from [HN] "We read the source code, job
   submission script, and the hardware"; the budget line for the department's pilot is the author's. Commitment's step,
   "run a two-week waste measurement on the cluster": [WB] "Two weeks on your cluster. A real wastage number. No
   commitment. If the numbers don't justify a pilot, you walk away with the report." (The same post also offers "a
   section of your cluster for a week"; the two weeks of the pricing paragraph and the site are used.)

6. **Mechanism.** An agent on every node, hooked into the scheduler; a cluster-specific model predicts what each job needs
   at submit time.
   [HN] "Expanse installs on every node and hooks into SLURM (or the K8s scheduler). It ingests live hardware telemetry
   (DCGM, CUPTI, Cgroups, Network/IO monitoring)". [HN] "We predict the GPU VRAM, Utilisation, memory, CPUs and walltime
   the job actually needs, with a confidence interval." [HN] "If a workload fails, we take all the data we collected and
   perform correlations on the stack profiling and the hardware telemetry". [LYC] "All analysis runs on your network."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`. Compatibility: the source code on the cluster beside the script
   (tested; the model reads it), the usual scheduler, Python ([HN] "currently only supported in python - other languages
   coming soon", of the profiler) — the conditions are the author's from these lines. Adoption friction: using the
   suggested sizes instead of padding (tested; [HN] "Our models are trained to over-provision rather than
   under-provision"), applying the code fixes. Relative advantage: [LYC] "Debug failures in seconds, not days"
   (fewer_attempts, the job runs first time) and a shorter queue wait for smaller requests (shorter_time, the author's
   reading of a smaller request fitting sooner); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** Per cluster a month, no figure; the cost is the share of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and
   never used.
   [HN] "We're currently onboarding customers as paid pilots. Pricing is determined per-cluster." No figure exists in
   [LYC], [HN], [WB] or [SITE] (no pricing page). The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a
   month**, is the operator's reading: for the smallest cluster the founders address (100 GPUs, about 73,000 GPU hours a
   month), [LYC]'s 30% reserved and unused is about 22,000 GPU hours, which at an assumed $2 to $3 a GPU hour (the
   author's assumption; [HN] prices its $8.5M "At on-demand cloud rates for the same hardware" without naming a rate) is
   about $44,000 to $66,000 a month; a fee of a fifth to a third of the waste on the smallest cluster is the author's
   choice. Existing sacrifice: RATE, about 30% to 59% of the cluster's GPU hours per cluster a month, the low from [LYC],
   the high from [HN]'s measured cluster. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent never compares with
   dollars), so the operators answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from the thread; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (a genomics user) "I do genomics work and my jobs tend to be bursty. They may use a lot of CPU initially, but the
   second half of the job is writing results. This takes only one core, but still the max amount of memory." [HN] (an
   HPC user) "I know from snooping on sumbit scripts and node utilization on the HPC that I use at my institution that
   most submissions leave some compute on the table (and many of them are egregiously bad)." [HN] (a student) "It's not
   trivial to estimate a priori the amount of time required for my simulation to complete, so I overestimate."

author's reading of a thread that agreed on the waste and argued about security and the business. No respondent
carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Status today

Same idea, five months after launch. [SITE] "Expanse delivers compute certainty. We predict exactly what every job
needs before it runs", still sales-led ("Book a discovery call"), now citing "$8M Monthly wastage uncovered" (a later
figure, not used). [YCP] lists the company as Spring 2026 with the Launch YC text. No public price today ([SITE] has no
pricing page, read 2026-10-22).

## Could not be sourced

- **A price figure.** None at launch or today; the founder's $10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month is the operator's
  (author's) reading, and the GPU-hour rate behind its arithmetic is an assumption.
- **The waste per cluster as an operator would read it.** The founders' 30% is an industry figure they cite and their
  59% is one national cluster; the operators' value boxes (20% to 60%) are the author's.
- **A buyer title and who has to agree.** [HN] names "datacenter operators" and "one department"; the decider role, the
  department head as the tested role and the security team are the author's reading.
- **A US market.** The founders are in Edinburgh; the US is the author's choice under rule U.
- **A researcher's hour.** No source; `hourly_rate` 60 is a round stand-in, unread by the RATE cost.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction conditions, the Purchase friction items but the security review, and every
  pick are the author's.

founder.order_why: The flow moves from market to context, then the problem's beliefs, stories and checks, then who asks and who gets the link, the same order I would explain Expanse to a researcher.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 carry the same kicker and question ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies'), so after the window screen it feels like the context screen comes back a second time.
founder.missing: The belief screens only ask whether and how often researchers guessed sizes, which is nearly everyone every day. They never ask what I actually believe is the pain: how much of a request sits idle (two to three times over-requested) or how often a job dies mid-run from guessing low.

PRIMARY.order_why: Screen 4 asks what I'd most like made easier before screen 5 has me recall how my last submission's guess actually went; I'd rather recount that submission first. Screens 1 and 2 also both say '1 of 4', which made me unsure where I was.
PRIMARY.asked_twice: Screens 2 and 3: 'did you guess' and then 'on how many days did you guess' are the same question, the second just counts it.
PRIMARY.missing: Nothing asked what happened when the guess was wrong. A job killed mid-run for running out of memory or hitting its time limit, how many hours or days of work were lost, and whether I had a checkpoint to resume from are what make this painful for me. It also didn't ask whether I pad my requests to avoid that, or how long that padding makes me wait in the queue.

screens.why1: After the cost and how often, asking how researchers handle sizing today is the obvious next question before testing whether that falls short.
screens.why2: It is in my own words, job, cluster, memory, GPUs and run time, and I can answer it at once, though 'wasting the cluster' is my shorthand rather than how a researcher would say it.
screens.why3: I know exactly what researchers do: they guess and pad two to three times so the job doesn't die mid-run, which is the core of my pitch.
screens.why4: The only option is the escape chip 'Leave this out of the study', which fits a founder who can't say; the two boxes take my act and my rungs cleanly.
screens.why5: Nothing is reworded; the question restates my job line, and my answer and three rungs stand as I typed them.
screens.why7: The boxes take the act and its means plus my rungs on one measure (how much of the request sat idle), the first rung a working one ('Ran first time, sized about right'); Keel can add the failed-partway and never-ran rungs to reach five, and the line can sit under my first rung by default.

screens.why1: Right after I said how my researchers size jobs today, checking the five outcomes Keel built from that is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: 'Sized about right', 'holding twice what it used', 'failed partway and had to be resubmitted' is how anyone on a SLURM cluster talks about a job.
screens.why3: These are exactly the outcomes I see in sacct and node telemetry every day: right-sized, padded 2-3x, OOM or walltime kill and resubmit, never finished.
screens.why4: The rungs are distinct and in my words, but the waste steps leave gaps: 'about twice' and 'three times' give no home to a job holding 1.5x, or to the 8-GPU copied script holding 4x or more.
screens.why5: These are my own rungs and my own numbers ('two to three times' over-request, 'kills your job mid-run'), kept as I typed them, and the box restates my belief.
screens.why7: There are five rungs, best to worst, with a working first rung and the line under it (1 against, 4 for), and the bar names the exact rung, so the belief can go either way; but the scale blends two costs (idle GPUs, then failure), and its capped multiples leave true answers like 4x or more without a rung.
screens.instead: Ran first time, sized about right · Ran, holding up to twice what it used · Ran, holding at least three times what it used · Failed partway and had to be resubmitted · Never ran to the end

screens.why1: Choosing who will ask my researchers the questions belongs right before the study goes out, after the problem rows are checked.
screens.why2: The question and hint are plain: two named interviewers, a 5-second preview of each, a one-off 400-credit charge either way, and the link sent by text.
screens.why3: Picking a voice from two previews is something I can do at a glance with no special knowledge.
screens.why4: Two distinct interviewers, each with a preview, and Daphne is preselected, so keeping the default needs no extra chip.
screens.why5: It keeps my word 'researchers' and leaks nothing about Expanse, the scheduler hook or the operators to the people who will be asked.

screens.why1: After choosing who asks the questions, choosing how researchers answer is the obvious next step before sending the link.
screens.why2: AI interviewer, read and tap, and let them choose are plain to me, and each line says exactly what the researcher would do.
screens.why3: I know my researchers sit at a terminal between submissions and would rather tap through a short form than talk to a video, so I can answer this from what I know of them.
screens.why4: The three options cover the whole choice, they don't overlap, they are in plain words, and no escape is needed for a founder's setting.
screens.why5: My pick 'Read and tap' is kept, and nothing of my product leaks into the respondent-facing description.

screens.why1: Once I've chosen how researchers answer, choosing who receives the link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: All three are plain to me as a founder: named people, a list from Keel's Contacts search, or one open link posted where researchers already gather, like a SLURM users' channel or an HPC centre's mailing list.
screens.why3: I know who I can reach: researchers I know by name at the clusters we've talked to, or the communities where they post.
screens.why4: The three ways of reaching people are distinct and complete, and each says who sends what; the only snag I'd notice is that the open link requires Google sign-in, which some researchers at national HPC centres may not have, but the option is still true and usable.
screens.why5: My pick, people I know by name each getting their own link, is shown as I chose it, and nothing about Expanse leaks into the choice.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right under the title with '4 counted' beside it, and the Frequency card spells out '5 needed', so I know it is one person short; it names only Frequency, though Importance and Current solution are equally short.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart on this page, but the tally reads plainly: 4 beliefs, 1 holding, 3 too few, 7 answered, and Prevalence's '6 of 7 · bar 6 of 7 · at the bar' shows the count, the base and where the bar sits.
screens.why_b3: These are my four dimensions and recognisably my beliefs, but Prevalence says 'ran time', and Importance still names my thing as 'Guessing memory, GPUs and run time' rather than sizing a job to neither fail nor waste GPUs.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' implies I should get more researchers to answer, but the page never says so, and the 'What it measures' footer is generic.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is in the kicker and the tally, three cards say outright that they are too few to call, and Prevalence at exactly 6 of 7 is called 'holding up', not strong.
screens.instead: Too few to call: Frequency, Importance and Current solution each have 4 of the 5 counted answers they need, so get a few more researchers to answer before reading the problem; Prevalence holds, but only just, at 6 of 7.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its number, 6 of 7 said yes against a bar of 6 of 7, at the bar, so I know where I stand and why.
screens.why_b2: The strip counts the 7 who answered the gate, 6 for and 1 against, with the marker at 6 on a 0 to 7 axis, so what is counted, over how many and where my bar sits are plain at once.
screens.why_b3: It is recognisable but not quite mine: my segment is cut to 'researchers and ML engineers' without the SLURM/Kubernetes 100+ GPU clusters, 'ran time' is a typo, and the line counts the guessing at submit, which every one of my researchers does, rather than the job that dies or the GPUs held idle that I actually counted.
screens.why_b4: Pointing me to Frequency and Importance is a pointer, not a meaning; it does not tell me this card only shows that people who submitted a job had to size it, which says nothing yet about waste.
screens.why_b5: The small group is said ('a lean, not a call'), but 'Holding up' on a gate that asks the guessing everyone does at submit (the only No was someone with no jobs that week) softly overstates support for my waste belief.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 had to size a job this week, at your bar of 8 in 10, a lean from 7; this asked whether they guessed, not whether a job failed or held idle GPUs, so whether the waste is common is the next cards' to say.

screens.why_b1: The status word 'Too few to call' sits right beside '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', so I know there is no verdict yet and the exact reason why.
screens.why_b2: The axis of working days and the median at 4 read at once, but the bar needs a second look: 'your bar · 4 of 5 (at least 2 in 3)' sits beside four cells already for me, and the axis starts at 0 though nobody past the gate could answer 0.
screens.why_b3: 'Guess a job's memory, GPUs and run time on 3 to 5 working days out of 5' is my circumstance and my range, and 'researchers and ML engineers' is my own segment's wording.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic; it does not say that one more counted researcher would decide it, or that all four so far lean my way.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (6 answered, 4 counted, the two not counted and why), and the small group is called 'a lean, not a call' rather than a hold.
screens.instead: Too few to call: all 4 counted researchers guessed on 3 or more of 5 days (middle 4); one more counted answer decides it, so get one more researcher on a shared cluster to answer.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Too few to call' sits right beside '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', so I know there is no verdict and exactly why.
screens.why_b2: The bars plainly count 8 picks from 4 people with my row on top at 3, but the strip's 'your bar · 4 of 5' next to only 4 counted cells takes a second look to see that it means 4 of the 5 needed, not 4 of the 4 I have.
screens.why_b3: It is recognisably my belief, but the own row is the old 'Guessing memory, GPUs and run time', which just repeats the circumstance, not my reworded 'Sizing a job to neither fail nor waste GPUs', while the allocation rival does show its new wording.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it does not say that 3 of my 4 counted researchers already put it in their two, or that one more counted answer that picks it would carry the bar.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the two uncounted people are named with the reason, and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' keeps a 3-of-4 lean from being read as a result.
screens.instead: 3 of the 4 researchers counted put sizing a job (neither fail nor waste GPUs) in their two, and Kwabena, who sizes from past runs, did not. One more counted answer decides it: if it picks sizing, the belief holds at 4 of 5.

screens.why_b1: 'Too few to call' sits right beside '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', so I know there is no verdict yet and exactly which number stops it.
screens.why_b2: The rungs, their counts and the line under 'Ran first time, sized about right' read at once, but the strip's 'your bar · 4 of 5' next to my 4 counted made me stop to work out that it means 4 of 5 would be needed, not that 4 of 5 landed.
screens.why_b3: Current solution, the act 'guessing memory, time and GPUs before submitting' and the top rung 'Ran first time, sized about right' are my own words, and 'researchers and ML engineers' is my segment.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is a generic line: it does not say that one more counted researcher would decide it, or that 3 of 4 already lean my way.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the two not counted are named with the reason, and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' keeps 3 of 4 from being sold as a held belief.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of the 4 counted fell short (two held three times what they used, one died partway), so it leans your way. One more counted researcher decides it, so get one more answer.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', so I know there is no verdict yet and exactly why.
screens.why_b3: Importance is my dimension, but the belief line still says 'Guessing memory, GPUs and run time' where I now word the item 'Sizing a job to neither fail nor waste GPUs'; it is recognisable but not the line I checked.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what to do: not that I need one more counted researcher, and not whether data movement and software setup should change the pitch or the item list.
screens.why_b5: The n stays visible (4 counted, 1 against, 1 asked), the low count is called 'too few to call', and the one quote is not stretched beyond the person who said it.
screens.why_b6: Kwabena's point adds something I did not write: sizing from last week's runs works for him, and his day goes to moving data onto the nodes and getting libraries to agree, which names the rival pains.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 of 5 counted. The one researcher against says sizing from past runs works and data movement and library setup cost more of their day. Get one more researcher's answer before reading this, and watch whether those two pains come up again.

screens.why1: As the first screen, it obviously checks whether I'm the right kind of person before asking about my jobs.
screens.why2: SLURM, Kubernetes, cluster and GPUs are everyday words in my work, so I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I know which scheduler I submit to and roughly how big our shared cluster is, so I can answer straight away.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it for a gate, and §5 says the gate has no escape, so none is missing.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment (SLURM or Kubernetes, 100 or more GPUs) and shows nothing of a product or plan.
screens.why6: It is one short question with no symbols or abbreviations that only the eye reads, and the two options are easy to hold.
screens.instead: In the last week, did you submit jobs to a SLURM or Kubernetes cluster with at least 100 GPUs? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after the screener on cluster use, asking about my last 5 working days of submitting jobs is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Memory, GPUs and run time are exactly the fields I fill in for sbatch or a pod spec, though I would say I 'requested' them rather than 'guessed' them.
screens.why3: I know whether I submitted a job this week and set its resources, so I can answer from my own work.
screens.why4: Yes and No are complete and distinct, and the chips belong to the story box after a Yes rather than to the gate.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks to me, but the screen drifts from the founder's problem: it asks the setup every submission involves instead of the costly thing going wrong, like a job killed mid-run for under-requesting or a reservation sized at the max and left idle.
screens.why6: One short question with a three-item list and 'Yes or no' at the end, easy to hold on one hearing.
screens.why7: The gate asks the circumstance and not the problem: every researcher who submitted a job this week set its memory, GPUs and run time, so everyone says Yes, No has no one, and the founder's band can never be refuted, as in the card's bad example.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did a job of yours get killed for running out of memory or time? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after I said yes to guessing a job's resources this week, asking on how many days that happened is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: I'd say I 'requested' or 'set' memory, GPUs and a time limit in the sbatch script; 'guess' is close to how it feels, but it leaves me wondering whether a day I just resubmitted an old script counts.
screens.why3: I know which days this week I submitted jobs and had to pick the numbers, so I can count them.
screens.why4: One button per working day from 1 to 5, with no zero after my yes, and 'I can't recall' kept apart is complete and fits.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's situation of having to guess memory, GPUs and run time before submitting, and nothing about a product or their own terms reaches me.
screens.why6: It is short and is one question, and 'a number from 1 to 5, or say you can't recall' is easy to hold when heard.
screens.why7: The measure is days of the window, the buttons run 1 to 5 with the count last, there is no zero, the single escape is 'I can't recall', and the clause stays within 8 words.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, on how many days did you set a job's memory, GPUs and time limit before submitting it? 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · I can't recall

screens.why1: After asking whether and how often I guessed a job's memory, GPUs and run time, it makes sense to ask how that compares with the other things that eat my week on the cluster.
screens.why2: Every option is in words I use daily: GPU-hour allocation, getting software working, waiting for a job to start; only 'your last run of jobs' is a little loose, but I know what it means.
screens.why3: These are exactly the things I fight with myself when I submit to the shared cluster, and I could pick from my last few days without guessing.
screens.why4: The rows are distinct tasks in my words, but 'Waiting for a job to start' and 'Keeping within the GPU-hour allocation' are partly caused by how big I guess my request, so they overlap a little with the guessing row.
screens.why5: No product or company term reaches me, and the resource-guessing row reads the same as the earlier screens about my own work.
screens.why6: Heard once, it is one short question and five parallel -ing phrases I can hold, with the escape said last; the GPU-hour allocation row is the longest but still says cleanly.
screens.why7: The measure, the five rows with the own item not first, the single 'None of these' escape and the room for the belief to be supported or refuted are all right, but the own row carries a list inside it (memory, GPUs and run time) and the queue and allocation rows sit close to being consequences of it.
screens.instead: Think of the jobs you submitted this week. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Moving data on and off the cluster · Staying within your group's GPU-hour allocation · Getting software working on the cluster · Guessing what resources a job needs · Waiting in the queue for a job to start · None of these

screens.why1: After asking which part of sizing I'd most like made easier, it's natural to ask how my last submission's guess actually turned out.
screens.why2: I know every word, but 'how did guessing ... go' is clumsy, because the guess itself doesn't go anywhere; what I'd answer is how the job went with what I asked for.
screens.why3: I size and submit my own jobs, so I know whether the last one ran, got killed or sat on far more memory than it used.
screens.why4: The rungs are mostly what really happens, but 'three times' leaves no place for a job that held four or ten times its use, and 'failed partway and had to be resubmitted' blurs into 'never ran to the end' for a killed job I haven't rerun yet.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product or the founder's terms reaches me; it's just my own sizing and what happened.
screens.why6: The five options say well as a list, but the stem's 'how did guessing memory, time and GPUs before submitting go' is a mouthful to take in at one hearing.
screens.why7: There is a working first rung, a failed-outright last rung, five rungs in order and the right escape, 'I can't recall', for a job I size myself, but the measure bends from how much the job over-held to whether it failed at all.
screens.instead: Think of the last job you submitted. How did the memory, GPUs and time you asked for turn out? Sized about right, ran to the end / Ran, asked for about twice what it used / Ran, asked for three times or more / Killed partway, had to resubmit / Never ran to the end; or I can't recall
